newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fresh scandals shake Belgium, more seen coming.
newsitem.headline: Fresh scandals shake Belgium, more seen coming.

text.p: Fresh scandal has hit Belgium, already reeling from revelations of paedophile murder and allegations of political power-peddling and legal laxity, and analysts warned on Monday there was more to come.

They said, however, that the government did not yet appear threatened by tales of official corruption which gained fresh impetus by the discovery last summer of four murdered girls and ensuing allegations of a high-level cover-up.

"We are sitting on a time-bomb, but Belgian politicians have proved themselves extremely clever in the past at defusing time-bombs," Lieven Dewinter, Professor of Political Science at the Catholic University of Louvain, told Reuters.
"I don't think the government will resign although certain individuals may have to. But these are replaceable," he added.

The scandals struck at the heart of government for the first time at the weekend as newspapers reported that Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo had been linked to police investigations into paedophilia -- acts he angrily denied, accusing opposition politicians of trying to undermine the government.
"Never have I been involved in this sort of thing. What is disgusting from some members of the opposition is that they are trying to use this in a political way," he told RTBF television.

"The minister has been accused of very horrible things," said Kris Deschouwer, Professor of Political Science at Brussels Free University. "But the resignation of the government would mean elections and I don't think the two main parties want elections now." The next national elections are due in 1999.

The scandals began in August with the arrest of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux and the subsequent rescue of two sexually abused girls, the discovery of the dead bodies of four more and the renewed hunt for at least seven others.

Accusations began flying as a catalogue of police bungling and rivalry between different teams of investigators was unveiled along with revelations of judicial dithering that highlighted the political promotion of magistrates.
With the spotlight and public anger focused firmly on both the judiciary and Belgium's creaking political apparatus, the two sides began slinging mud at each other.

"There is almost war between the political sphere and the judicial sphere," Deschouwer said. "It can stop here or it can continue, but I don't think that the general mood will disappear quickly. We are in for a few more months of this."
Dewinter agreed. "Both sides are under fire so both could have an interest in highlighting the inefficiencies of the other in order to deflect attention. So more cases can come out."
Both men drew parallels with the hurricane of change that swept through the Italian political establishment.

Both also warned, however, that the similarities were superficial given Belgium's linguistic divide, which rules out a simple majority approach to instituting change, and the lack of political alternatives waiting in the wings.
"We do not have a majority culture," Dewinter said.

Both Deschouwer and Dewinter said change was inevitable and would be accelerated by political infighting coinciding with public demands, but they said it was impossible to forecast where those changes would lead.

"It is clear that things have not completely changed and there are some nasty things from the past still being discovered," Deschouwer said. "So I think we are going through a phase of cleaning up the remainders of the old system.

"If you shake the political tree to get rid of a few dead leaves you risk all the branches falling off and I do not see alternatives for the existing parties or the political system in Belgium," he added.

Dewinter and Deschouwer warned against what they described as a mood in Belgium verging on that in the anti-communist Macarthyite era in the United States in the 1950s with a simple hint of scandal being enough to inflict a fatal wound.
"At the moment we are getting guilt by association rather than guilt by proof and this sort of thing is extremely difficult to stop. You can drop any name you like," Deschouwer said.
"A number of these things will obviously be true, and what is difficult is making the distinction between what is true and relevant and what is just name dropping trying to kill the other," he added.
"It is a good time to try to go and kill."
